title: Anne Wojcicki, the FDA's Warning Letter and Fifteen Months of Steps
dek: In November 2013 regulators told 23andMe to stop marketing its health reports; Anne Wojcicki complied and rebuilt them one authorised test at a time.

story.event: Halting health reports after the FDA's November 2013 warning letter and seeking authorisation test by test
story.summary: On 22 November 2013 the FDA ordered 23andMe to stop marketing its Personal Genome Service, saying the company had not shown its health reports were valid and had stopped communicating. On 5 December 23andMe stopped giving health results to new customers and sold only ancestry information and raw data; in February 2015 the FDA authorised its Bloom syndrome carrier test, and health reports returned in October 2015. The company filed for bankruptcy in 2025 and its assets were sold to a nonprofit led by Wojcicki.
paragraphs: On 22 November 2013 the US Food and Drug Administration sent a warning letter to Anne Wojcicki, chief executive of 23andMe in California. Her company sold a $99 saliva kit and advertised "health reports on 254 diseases and conditions." The agency wrote that it had worked with 23andMe since July 2009, through more than 14 meetings and calls and hundreds of emails, but had heard nothing since May while the company launched television advertising. It must immediately stop marketing the service. A false breast-cancer risk result, the letter warned, could lead someone to preventive surgery.

Wojcicki later said the company had at first believed it would not need FDA approval, since it ran under the laboratory rules covering most genetic tests; by 2010, she said, it understood it would be regulated as a medical device, "but there was a lot of miscommunication on our behalf." Within days 23andMe admitted it had not met the agency's expectations on timeline and communication. At a Fortune event in San Francisco she said: "Big challenges are an accumulation of small challenges."

Late on 5 December the company said it would comply. People who bought kits from 22 November onward would receive ancestry information and their raw genetic data with no health interpretation; earlier customers kept their reports. Wojcicki said the aim was to work cooperatively with the FDA.

The return was slow. She relied on Kathy Hibbs, the company's chief legal and regulatory officer, and found herself in Washington often: "We weren't in D.C. enough before." In February 2015 the FDA authorised 23andMe's Bloom syndrome carrier test, the first direct-to-consumer genetic test it had cleared. Staff gave a standing ovation, she recalled. "There is a level of steps and patience that is required." In October 2015 the service returned with dozens of health reports, and in April 2017 the FDA allowed risk reports for ten conditions, including Parkinson's disease.

The company later went public but struggled to become profitable. After a 2023 data breach and the resignation of its independent directors in 2024, it filed for bankruptcy in March 2025 and Wojcicki resigned as chief executive. That summer a court approved the sale of its assets for $305 million to TTAM Research Institute, a nonprofit she leads.

quote.text: Be not disgusted, nor discouraged, nor dissatisfied, if thou dost not succeed in doing everything according to right principles, but when thou hast failed, return back again, and be content if the greater part of what thou doest is consistent with man's nature
quote.source_title: Thoughts of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #15877
quote.connection: Marcus allows for failure but asks for a return without disgust or despair. Wojcicki's answer to the letter was that kind of return: admitting the lapse, narrowing what the company offered, and coming back one authorised test at a time.

reflection: The FDA's complaint was not that 23andMe's idea was wrong. It was that the company had not shown its tests worked, and had stopped answering. You know that gap: a method that seems to work is not yet a validated one, and silence towards someone who checks your work rarely stays neutral.

When something you are responsible for falls short, there is a pull either to defend it or to give it up. Wojcicki took a third way: name the gap, promise less for a while, and start answering again. It took fifteen months to win one test back, and it began with a reply.
invitation: Think of one message from someone who checks your work, a supervisor, an assessor or a client, that you have been slow to answer. Send two lines today saying where things stand and when you will follow up.

The decision: on 5 December 2013 23andMe stopped health interpretation for customers who bought from 22 November, offering only ancestry and raw data
The company acknowledged communication failures with the FDA
In February 2015 the FDA authorised 23andMe's Bloom syndrome carrier test, the first direct-to-consumer genetic test it authorised

research_notes: What Wojcicki knew about regulation: in PLOS Genetics (2015) she said the company originally thought it would not need FDA approval because it operated under CLIA; to KQED (April 2015) she said it understood 'even back in 2010' that it would be regulated as a medical device. The FDA letter says it had been working with the company since July 2009. The story gives both of her statements as hers, in sequence. The admission about 'timeline and communication' is a company statement reported by MIT Technology Review, not attributed to Wojcicki personally; Fortune paraphrases her as saying the company fell behind schedule and failed to communicate proactively. Refunds: Engadget's first version said post-22 November buyers would get refunds, then updated on 7 December to say kits were still sold with ancestry and raw data; the story does not mention refunds. Timing of the 5 December announcement: NPR says 'late Thursday' (5 December); some outlets date it 6 December. Customer numbers are not used in the story: Fortune (2013) gives a goal of one million by end of 2013; KQED (2015) says more than 850,000; for 2025 AP cites about 13 million from court documents and ABC says roughly 15 million. The court approval of the sale is dated Friday 27 June 2025 by AP and Monday by ABC (which reports the company's announcement), so the story says 'that summer'. The bankruptcy and sale are stated factually; no blame is attributed. The FDA letter and press releases are cited from Internet Archive copies because the current fda.gov URLs no longer serve them; their kind is given as 'court-record' as the nearest category for official regulatory records. Marcus Aurelius is writing about his own philosophical practice; it is applied to a company's regulatory recovery by analogy.
